papers.core_contribution: This paper challenges the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff by showing that monosemantic features not only enhance interpretability but also provide concrete gains in model robustness across various scenarios including noise, few-shot learning, and out-of-domain generalization.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that monosemanticity offers advantages beyond interpretability, improving model robustness across multiple learning scenarios, and advocates for exploring its broader learning benefits.
papers.key_findings:
Monosemantic features (from NCL or SAE) are more robust than polysemantic features under linear probing with label noise and input noise.
Maintaining monosemanticity during finetuning (via non-negative tuning) reduces overfitting and improves performance in few-shot and noisy-label settings.
MonoLoRA, a sparse variant of LoRA, better preserves alignment safety while maintaining task performance when finetuning LLMs on small datasets.
Empirical analysis shows that classifiers with higher robustness under noise rely more on monosemantic features.
Theoretical analysis on a toy model indicates monosemantic features have better linear separability under noise, leading to more robust decision boundaries.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models often suffer from a lack of interpretability due to polysemanticity, where individual neurons are activated by multiple unrelated semantics, resulting in unclear attributions of model behavior. Recent advances in monosemanticity, where neurons correspond to consistent and distinct semantics, have significantly improved interpretability but are commonly believed to compromise accuracy. In this work, we challenge the prevailing belief of the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff, showing that monosemantic features not only enhance interpretability but also bring concrete gains in model performance. Across multiple robust learning scenarios-including input and label noise, few-shot learning, and out-of-domain generalization-our results show that models leveraging monosemantic features significantly outperform those relying on polysemantic features. Furthermore, we provide empirical and theoretical understandings on the robustness gains of feature monosemanticity. Our preliminary analysis suggests that monosemanticity, by promoting better separation of feature representations, leads to more robust decision boundaries. This diverse evidence highlights the generality of monosemanticity in improving model robustness. As a first step in this new direction, we embark on exploring the learning benefits of monosemanticity beyond interpretability, supporting the long-standing hypothesis of linking interpretability and robustness. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/PKU-ML/Beyond_Interpretability}.

papers.title: Toy Models of Superposition
papers.research_question: Why do neurons sometimes align with interpretable features and sometimes not, and how can neural networks represent more features than they have dimensions (superposition)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that superposition—where neural networks store more sparse features than dimensions—is a real phenomenon, explains polysemanticity, and reveals a phase change and geometric structure in feature representations.
papers.conclusion: Superposition occurs in neural networks, allowing them to represent more features than dimensions, which has important implications for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Superposition is a real, observed phenomenon in neural networks.
Both monosemantic and polysemantic neurons can form.
At least some kinds of computation can be performed in superposition.
Whether features are stored in superposition is governed by a phase change.
Superposition organizes features into geometric structures such as digons, triangles, pentagons, and tetrahedrons.
papers.limitation:
The toy models are simple and it is unclear what to generalize to real networks.
The ReLU hidden layer toy model has a weakness where the model circumvents the activation function if possible.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often pack many unrelated concepts into a single neuron - a puzzling phenomenon known as 'polysemanticity' which makes interpretability much more challenging. This paper provides a toy model where polysemanticity can be fully understood, arising as a result of models storing additional sparse features in "superposition." We demonstrate the existence of a phase change, a surprising connection to the geometry of uniform polytopes, and evidence of a link to adversarial examples. We also discuss potential implications for mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Rethinking LLM-as-a-Judge: Representation-as-a-Judge with Small Language Models via Semantic Capacity Asymmetry
papers.research_question: Can small language models serve as efficient evaluators by leveraging internal representations, even when their generation is poor?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis and introduces INSPECTOR, a probing-based framework that extracts evaluation signals from small model representations, enabling efficient and accurate reference-free evaluation.
papers.conclusion: Small LMs retain strong evaluative signals in their internal representations, and the Representation-as-a-Judge paradigm via INSPECTOR offers a scalable and interpretable solution for evaluation and data curation.
papers.key_findings:
Small LMs encode rich evaluative signals in their hidden states despite weak generation.
Probing internal representations with INSPECTOR outperforms prompt-based evaluation with small LMs and closely approximates large LLM judges.
The Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis is supported: evaluation requires less semantic capacity than generation.
Probing classifiers can serve as reliable data filters for supervised fine-tuning, leading to performance gains.
Larger LLMs do not necessarily provide stronger evaluation signals than smaller ones.
papers.limitation:
Multiclass prediction performance of probing classifiers is modest (50-60%) compared to binary classification.
Out-of-distribution generalization for multiclass probing is limited, with F1 scores dropping significantly.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as reference-free evaluators via prompting, but this "LLM-as-a-Judge" paradigm is costly, opaque, and sensitive to prompt design. In this work, we investigate whether smaller models can serve as efficient evaluators by leveraging internal representations instead of surface generation. We uncover a consistent empirical pattern: small LMs, despite with weak generative ability, encode rich evaluative signals in their hidden states. This motivates us to propose the Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis: evaluation requires significantly less semantic capacity than generation and can be grounded in intermediate representations, suggesting that evaluation does not necessarily need to rely on large-scale generative models but can instead leverage latent features from smaller ones. Our findings motivate a paradigm shift from LLM-as-a-Judge to Representation-as-a-Judge, a decoding-free evaluation strategy that probes internal model structure rather than relying on prompted output. We instantiate this paradigm through INSPECTOR, a probing-based framework that predicts aspect-level evaluation scores from small model representations. Experiments on reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, GPQA) show that INSPECTOR substantially outperforms prompting-based small LMs and closely approximates full LLM judges, while offering a more efficient, reliable, and interpretable alternative for scalable evaluation.

papers.title: Language Through a Prism: A Spectral Approach for Multiscale Language\n Representations
papers.research_question: To what extent do deep models capture information at different scales (from subwords to documents), and can we force them to better capture structure across this hierarchy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a spectral filtering framework to disentangle scale-specific information in language model representations and a prism layer that trains models to specialize neurons for different scales, improving performance on long-range tasks.
papers.conclusion: Spectral techniques are a powerful set of tools for uncovering and modeling multiscale phenomena in deep NLP models.
papers.key_findings:
Spectral filters can disentangle scale-specific information in BERT representations, with high-pass filters useful for word-level tasks and low-pass filters for document-level tasks.
The prism layer enables BERT to produce multiscale representations that improve performance on utterance- and document-level tasks while maintaining word-level performance.
Training with the prism layer increases the model's sensitivity to long-range context in masked language modeling.
The method is general and could be applied to other domains like images, audio, and video.
future_direction: Applying the spectral techniques to other domains such as computer vision, time series, and reinforcement learning models.
Using the tools for interpretability research to better understand knowledge and information processing at different scales.
Applying the method to track topics over time in linguistic change research.
papers.abstract:
Language exhibits structure at different scales, ranging from subwords to
words, sentences, paragraphs, and documents. To what extent do deep models
capture information at these scales, and can we force them to better capture
structure across this hierarchy? We approach this question by focusing on
individual neurons, analyzing the behavior of their activations at different
timescales. We show that signal processing provides a natural framework for
separating structure across scales, enabling us to 1) disentangle
scale-specific information in existing embeddings and 2) train models to learn
more about particular scales. Concretely, we apply spectral filters to the
activations of a neuron across an input, producing filtered embeddings that
perform well on part of speech tagging (word-level), dialog speech acts
classification (utterance-level), or topic classification (document-level),
while performing poorly on the other tasks. We also present a prism layer for
training models, which uses spectral filters to constrain different neurons to
model structure at different scales. Our proposed BERT + Prism model can better
predict masked tokens using long-range context and produces multiscale
representations that perform better at utterance- and document-level tasks. Our
methods are general and readily applicable to other domains besides language,
such as images, audio, and video.

papers.title: Exploration and adaptation of large language models for specialized domains
papers.research_question: Can large language models overcome challenges in specialized domains, and how can they be effectively adapted to domain-specific requirements?
papers.core_contribution: The dissertation provides insights into the inner workings of LLMs and proposes adaptation methods that demonstrate LLMs can be effectively used in specialized domains, particularly clinical NLP.
papers.conclusion: The work provides new insights into the inner workings of pre-trained language models and multiple adaptation methods showing that LLMs can be an effective tool for NLP in specialized domains.
papers.key_findings:
Layers of Transformer-based LLMs encode different dimensions of input text, with contextual representations and general language knowledge being beneficial for complex tasks.
Pre-trained language models outperform traditional approaches on clinical tasks.
Integration of domain-specific resources (like ICD hierarchy) improves model generalization.
Behavioral testing framework can serve as a tool for communication with domain experts.
Prototypical networks can provide interpretable diagnosis predictions.
papers.limitation: There is no ground truth in clinical data
future_direction: Integration of multimodal and multilingual data
Efficient methods for large language models
papers.abstract: Large language models have transformed the field of natural language processing (NLP). Their improved performance on various NLP benchmarks makes them a promising tool—also for the application in specialized domains. Such domains are characterized by highly trained professionals with particular domain expertise. Since these experts are rare, improving the efficiency of their work with automated systems is especially desirable. However, domain-specific text resources hold various challenges for NLP systems. These challenges include distinct language, noisy and scarce data, and a high level of variation. Further, specialized domains present an increased need for transparent systems since they are often applied in high stakes settings. In this dissertation, we examine whether large language models (LLMs) can overcome some of these challenges and propose methods to effectively adapt them to domain-specific requirements. We first investigate the inner workings and abilities of LLMs and show how they can fill the gaps that are present in previous NLP algorithms for specialized domains. To this end, we explore the sources of errors produced by earlier systems to identify which of them can be addressed by using LLMs. Following this, we take a closer look at how information is processed within Transformer-based LLMs to better understand their capabilities. We find that their layers encode different dimensions of the input text. Here, the contextual vector representation, and the general language knowledge learned during pre-training are especially beneficial for solving complex and multi-step tasks common in specialized domains. Following this exploration, we propose solutions for further adapting LLMs to the requirements of domain-specific tasks. We focus on the clinical domain, which incorporates many typical challenges found in specialized domains. We show how to improve generalization by integrating different domain-specific resources into our models. We further analyze the behavior of the produced models and propose a behavioral testing framework that can serve as a tool for communication with domain experts. Finally, we present an approach for incorporating the benefits of LLMs while fulfilling requirements such as interpretability and modularity. The presented solutions show improvements in performance on benchmark datasets and in manually conducted analyses with medical professionals. Our work provides both new insights into the inner workings of pre-trained language models as well as multiple adaptation methods showing that LLMs can be an effective tool for NLP in specialized domains.

papers.title: Are language models aware of the road not taken? Token-level uncertainty and hidden state dynamics
papers.research_question: Do language models represent the alternate paths they could take during generation? How do hidden activations correlate with token-level uncertainty and steering success?
papers.core_contribution: Hidden activations in language models correlate with token-level uncertainty and can be used to steer generation and predict future outcome distributions, indicating that models implicitly represent alternate reasoning paths.
papers.conclusion: Hidden activations in language models reflect token-level uncertainty and can be used to estimate outcome distributions efficiently, offering a way to understand and control model decision-making.
papers.key_findings:
Steering success correlates with token-level uncertainty: models are most steerable when they are least certain about the final answer.
Hidden activations contain information about the model's future outcome distribution, as linear probes on the model's own activations predict outcome distribution better than probes on another model's embeddings.
The dynamics of steering success and outcome distribution are similar, with abrupt changes at the same token positions identified by change point detection.
The correlation between steering success and base outcome probability is moderate (R=0.57) and consistent across examples (average R=0.64).
Linear probes are most predictive in middle layers (layers 6-10) of the model.
papers.limitation:
The computational cost of Forking Paths Analysis is high, requiring millions of tokens to analyze a single base path completion.
Only a handful of examples from three datasets are analyzed due to computational constraints.
papers.abstract: When a language model generates text, the selection of individual tokens might lead it down very different reasoning paths, making uncertainty difficult to quantify. In this work, we consider whether reasoning language models represent the alternate paths that they could take during generation. To test this hypothesis, we use hidden activations to control and predict a language model's uncertainty during chain-of-thought reasoning. In our experiments, we find a clear correlation between how uncertain a model is at different tokens, and how easily the model can be steered by controlling its activations. This suggests that activation interventions are most effective when there are alternate paths available to the model -- in other words, when it has not yet committed to a particular final answer. We also find that hidden activations can predict a model's future outcome distribution, demonstrating that models implicitly represent the space of possible paths.

papers.title: Emergence of Biological Structural Discovery in General-Purpose Language Models
papers.research_question: Can general-purpose language models infer biological structural logic through abstract reasoning without domain-specific training, or is it dependent on massive biological data?
papers.core_contribution: General-purpose language models possess an emergent capability for biological structural discovery through cross-modal transfer from linguistic syntax, enabling zero-shot performance on tasks like protein homology detection without domain-specific training.
papers.conclusion: The deep isomorphism between human language and biological sequences suggests that syntax is a universal property of organized information, and general-purpose LLMs can serve as powerful probes for decoding biological structure without domain-specific training.
papers.key_findings:
A GPT-2 model fine-tuned on English paraphrasing achieves ~84% zero-shot accuracy in protein homology detection, demonstrating cross-modal syntactic transfer.
Scaling to large models like Qwen-3 reveals a phase transition to near-perfect accuracy on standard tasks and maintains 75% precision on remote homology datasets.
Chain-of-Thought analysis shows that models perform 'mental folding', leveraging implicit structural knowledge for reasoning beyond sequence alignment.
The capability extends to DNA homology and Central Dogma mapping, with performance varying based on model scale and pre-training exposure.
The BioPAWS benchmark is introduced to standardize evaluation of cross-modal biological understanding in LLMs.
papers.limitation: Generative tasks such as de novo design of functional enzymes may lead to biologically plausible but physically unstable structures due to hallucinations.
future_direction: Hybrid architecture using general LLMs as high-level architects and domain-specific models as engineers to enforce physical constraints.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large language models (LLMs) are evolving into engines for scientific discovery, yet the assumption that biological understanding requires domain-specific pre-training remains unchallenged. Here, we report that general-purpose LLMs possess an emergent capability for biological structural discovery. First, we demonstrate that a small-scale GPT-2, fine-tuned solely on English paraphrasing, achieves ~84% zero-shot accuracy in protein homology detection, where network-based interpretability confirms a deep structural isomorphism between human language and the language of life. Scaling to massive models (e.g., Qwen-3) reveals a phase transition, achieving near-perfect accuracy (~100%) on standard tasks while maintaining 75% precision on specially constructed remote homology datasets. Chain-of-Thought interpretability reveals that these models transcend simple sequence alignment, leveraging implicit structural knowledge to perform reasoning akin to "mental folding." We formalize this cross-modal universality through the BioPAWS benchmark. Our work establishes a minimalist paradigm for AI for Science, proving that abstract logical structures distilled from human language constitute a powerful cognitive prior for decoding the complex syntax of biology.

papers.title: Schema-learning and rebinding as mechanisms of in-context learning and emergence
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning work, and can it be explained through schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in interpretable models like clone-structured causal graphs (CSCGs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that in-context learning can be achieved through schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in interpretable clone-structured causal graphs, providing insights into how ICL works in large language models.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in CSCGs can explain in-context learning, offering insights for designing interpretable architectures and understanding emergence in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
CSCG achieves in-context learning on the GINC dataset, accurately retrieving latent concepts.
CSCG learns template circuits for algorithms and generalizes to novel tokens through rebinding on the LIALT dataset.
ICL performance improves with model overparameterization, suggesting emergence is related to capacity.
CSCG can inductively learn new word usage from single examples in the dax test.
The mechanisms of schema-learning and rebinding in CSCGs provide a plausible explanation for ICL in transformers.
papers.limitation:
CSCG fails to generalize to concepts unseen during training, similar to transformers.
Imperfections in learned CSCG models can lead to failure cases, such as wrong schema retrieval.
future_direction: Designing novel architectures based on schema-learning and rebinding principles.
Searching for interpretable and editable circuits in transformers using the identified mechanisms.
Extending the approach to more complex tasks and datasets.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is one of the most powerful and most unexpected capabilities to emerge in recent transformer-based large language models (LLMs). Yet the mechanisms that underlie it are poorly understood. In this paper, we demonstrate that comparable ICL capabilities can be acquired by an alternative sequence prediction learning method using clone-structured causal graphs (CSCGs). Moreover, a key property of CSCGs is that, unlike transformer-based LLMs, they are {\em interpretable}, which considerably simplifies the task of explaining how ICL works. Specifically, we show that it uses a combination of (a) learning template (schema) circuits for pattern completion, (b) retrieving relevant templates in a context-sensitive manner, and (c) rebinding of novel tokens to appropriate slots in the templates. We go on to marshall evidence for the hypothesis that similar mechanisms underlie ICL in LLMs. For example, we find that, with CSCGs as with LLMs, different capabilities emerge at different levels of overparameterization, suggesting that overparameterization helps in learning more complex template (schema) circuits. By showing how ICL can be achieved with small models and datasets, we open up a path to novel architectures, and take a vital step towards a more general understanding of the mechanics behind this important capability.

papers.title: Inducing Causal World Models in LLMs for Zero-Shot Physical Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can we induce a causal world model in Large Language Models to improve zero-shot physical reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Causal World Model Induction (CWMI) framework, which augments a frozen LLM with a trainable Causal Physics Module and a Causal Intervention Loss to learn cause-and-effect relationships, significantly improving zero-shot physical reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Inducing an explicit causal world model within an LLM via the CWMI framework is a critical and effective step towards building AI systems with robust, generalizable physical reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
CWMI achieves 89.4% zero-shot accuracy on PIQA, outperforming Llama 3 8B (74.2%) and GPT-4 (85.5%).
On the novel PhysiCa-Bench, CWMI achieves 94.1% accuracy, 87.6% Causal Consistency Score, and a low Future State Prediction Error (MSE 0.08).
Ablation studies show the Causal Intervention Loss is critical for causal consistency, and the State Prediction Loss is necessary for grounding predictions in physical reality.
The two-component architecture (frozen LLM + trainable CPM) is more effective than fine-tuning the LLM directly, validating the modular design.
Performance scales with CPM capacity, plateauing at around 256M parameters for the rigid-body dynamics in the benchmark.
papers.limitation:
Struggles with complex multi-object interactions (e.g., a pile of falling blocks).
Cannot handle non-rigid and fluid dynamics, as training was on rigid-body physics.
Fails when key physical properties are not explicitly stated or strongly implied in the text (e.g., implicit understanding that a feather has high air resistance).
future_direction: Architectural enhancements to the CPM, such as adopting graph neural networks for multi-object tracking.
Incorporating physics-informed neural network techniques for continuous fields like fluids.
Integrating more sophisticated 3D visual representations.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), despite their advanced linguistic capabilities, fundamentally lack an intuitive understanding of physical dynamics, which limits their effectiveness in real-world scenarios that require causal reasoning. In this paper, we introduce Causal World Model Induction (CWMI), a novel framework designed to embed an explicit model of causal physics within an LLM. Our approach incorporates a dedicated Causal Physics Module (CPM) and a new training objective called Causal Intervention Loss, encouraging the model to learn cause-and-effect relationships from multimodal data. By training the model to predict the outcomes of hypothetical interventions instead of merely capturing statistical correlations, CWMI develops a robust internal representation of physical laws. Experimental results show that CWMI significantly outperforms state-of-the-art LLMs on zero-shot physical reasoning tasks, including the PIQA benchmark and our newly proposed PhysiCa-Bench dataset. These findings demonstrate that inducing a causal world model is a critical step toward more reliable and generalizable AI systems.

papers.title: Is attention required for ICL? Exploring the Relationship Between Model Architecture and In-Context Learning Ability
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between model architecture and in-context learning ability? Which architectures are capable of ICL and which exhibit superior performance?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that in-context learning is not exclusive to attention-based models; all tested architectures can perform ICL, with some attention alternatives being competitive with or better than transformers in certain tasks.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning is not exclusive to attention-based models; all tested architectures can perform ICL, with attention alternatives being competitive. However, no architecture is consistent across all tasks, and performance degrades with out-of-distribution prompt lengths.
papers.key_findings:
All considered architectures can perform in-context learning, demonstrating ICL is not exclusive to attention-based models.
Attention alternatives such as Mamba, Hyena, RetNet, and RWKV are sometimes competitive with or better than transformers at ICL.
Performance varies with number of in-context examples; some architectures show degradation when extrapolating to longer prompts than seen in training.
The emergence of ICL in image classification is influenced by burstiness in training data; some architectures are predisposed towards memorization over ICL.
ICL score in language modeling correlates with performance on other ICL tasks, but not perfectly.
papers.abstract: What is the relationship between model architecture and the ability to perform in-context learning? In this empirical study, we take the first steps toward answering this question. We evaluate thirteen model architectures capable of causal language modeling across a suite of synthetic in-context learning tasks. These selected architectures represent a broad range of paradigms, including recurrent and convolution-based neural networks, transformers, state space model inspired, and other emerging attention alternatives. We discover that all the considered architectures can perform in-context learning under a wider range of conditions than previously documented. Additionally, we observe stark differences in statistical efficiency and consistency by varying the number of in-context examples and task difficulty. We also measure each architecture's predisposition towards in-context learning when presented with the option to memorize rather than leverage in-context examples. Finally, and somewhat surprisingly, we find that several attention alternatives are sometimes competitive with or better in-context learners than transformers. However, no single architecture demonstrates consistency across all tasks, with performance either plateauing or declining when confronted with a significantly larger number of in-context examples than those encountered during gradient-based training.

papers.title: Do Llamas understand the periodic table?
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) represent the periodic table of elements, and what is the geometric structure of their hidden states?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally develop structured geometric representations (a 3D spiral) of the periodic table in their hidden states, with knowledge encoded as continuous manifolds in middle layers that sharpen into categorical distinctions in deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: LLMs represent symbolic scientific knowledge as coherent, geometry-aware manifolds that reflect the natural order of the physical world, which can inform interpretability and trust in LLMs for scientific applications.
papers.key_findings:
A 3D spiral structure in LLM hidden states aligns with the conceptual organization of the periodic table.
Middle layers encode continuous, overlapping attribute subspaces, while deeper layers sharpen decision boundaries and integrate linguistic context.
Linguistic structure increasingly shapes factual representations in later layers.
Strong linear associations between related attributes in middle layers enable indirect recall.
Regression probing shows continuous numerical features are effectively represented in intermediate layers, while classification probing shows later layers are better for fine-grained categorical decisions.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to chemical elements in the periodic table; future studies could expand to other chemical structures and properties.
The hypothesis-driven validation of geometric structures may oversimplify LLMs' non-linear interactions.
future_direction: Expand to other chemical structures and properties.
Further investigation into how LLMs represent and reason about scientific knowledge.
papers.abstract: We observe a 3D spiral structure in the hidden states of LLMs that aligns with the conceptual structure of the periodic table.

papers.title: Sparse Reward Subsystem in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does there exist a sparse reward subsystem in LLM hidden states analogous to the biological reward subsystem, and what are its properties?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sparse reward subsystem in LLM hidden states, consisting of value neurons that encode state value and dopamine neurons that encode reward prediction error, and shows their critical role in reasoning and their robustness across models and tasks.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess a sparse reward subsystem analogous to the biological reward subsystem, which is consistent across tasks, layers, model scales, and architectures, and has potential applications.
papers.key_findings:
Value neurons exist in LLM hidden states and can predict the value of the current state using only a small fraction of neurons.
Ablating even 1% of value neurons severely impairs reasoning performance, while random ablation does not.
Value neurons are robust across diverse datasets, model scales, layers, and architectural designs.
Value neurons are transferable across different datasets and across models fine-tuned from the same base model.
Dopamine neurons exist and encode reward prediction error, with activation patterns correlating with positive and negative surprises.
papers.limitation: Dopamine neurons are demonstrated primarily through case studies rather than quantitative metrics.
future_direction: Further explore applications of the reward subsystem for detecting and guiding LLM generation and reasoning.
Develop quantitative metrics for measuring dopamine neurons.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify a sparse reward subsystem within the hidden states of Large Language Models (LLMs), drawing an analogy to the biological reward subsystem in the human brain. We demonstrate that this subsystem contains value neurons that represent the model's internal expectation of state value, and through intervention experiments, we establish the importance of these neurons for reasoning. Our experiments reveal that these value neurons are robust across diverse datasets, model scales, and architectures; furthermore, they exhibit significant transferability across different datasets and models fine-tuned from the same base model. By examining cases where value predictions and actual rewards diverge, we identify dopamine neurons within the reward subsystem which encode reward prediction errors (RPE). These neurons exhibit high activation when the reward is higher than expected and low activation when the reward is lower than expected.

papers.title: Hyperdimensional Probe: Decoding LLM Representations via Vector Symbolic Architectures
papers.research_question: How do LLMs represent concepts internally during analogy completion and text generation? Can VSA-based probing capture these latent features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Hyperdimensional Probe, a VSA-based probing method that unifies input-oriented feature extraction and output-oriented analysis to decode LLM representations.
papers.conclusion: The Hyperdimensional Probe successfully captures latent features in LLM representations using VSA, unifying prior probing methods and providing insights into conceptual representations during inference.
papers.key_findings:
The Hyperdimensional Probe effectively extracts meaningful concepts from LLM representations across diverse models and tasks.
Models differ in conceptual richness; e.g., OLMo-2 shows richer structure than GPT-2.
Mathematical analogies tend to have sparser conceptual representations.
During text generation, LLM failures may be due to loss of question-related concepts rather than answer-related concepts.
The method unifies input and output perspectives, enabling joint analysis.
papers.limitation: Dependence on unidirectional transformation that prevents causal validation and on a set of predefined features.
papers.abstract: Despite their capabilities, Large Language Models (LLMs) remain opaque with limited understanding of their internal representations. Current interpretability methods either focus on input-oriented feature extraction, such as supervised probes and Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), or on output distribution inspection, such as logit-oriented approaches. A full understanding of LLM vector spaces, however, requires integrating both perspectives, something existing approaches struggle with due to constraints on latent feature definitions. We introduce the Hyperdimensional Probe, a hybrid supervised probe that combines symbolic representations with neural probing. Leveraging Vector Symbolic Architectures (VSAs) and hypervector algebra, it unifies prior methods: the top-down interpretability of supervised probes, SAE's sparsity-driven proxy space, and output-oriented logit investigation. This allows deeper input-focused feature extraction while supporting output-oriented investigation. Our experiments show that our method consistently extracts meaningful concepts across LLMs, embedding sizes, and setups, uncovering concept-driven patterns in analogy-oriented inference and QA-focused text generation. By supporting joint input-output analysis, this work advances semantic understanding of neural representations while unifying the complementary perspectives of prior methods.

papers.title: The Evolution of Statistical Induction Heads: In-Context Learning Markov Chains
papers.research_question: How does the in-context learning capability emerge in transformers, specifically for learning Markov chains?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the ICL-MC task as a controlled setting to study in-context learning, showing transformers learn 'statistical induction heads' through phase transitions, and that simplicity bias can delay learning the optimal solution.
papers.conclusion: The ICL-MC task provides a useful controlled setting for understanding in-context learning and the emergence of statistical induction heads, revealing that networks pass through discrete incomplete solutions which may affect the speed of learning more complex circuits.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers learn statistical induction heads to optimally solve the in-context Markov chain task.
Learning occurs in phases: an initial uniform phase, a unigram phase, and a final bigram phase with a rapid transition between them.
The model's bias towards simpler (unigram) solutions can slow down the learning of the optimal bigram solution.
The alignment between the transformer's layers is crucial for the phase transition to the correct solution.
During training, positional embeddings develop an alternating pattern, with a bias towards looking back an odd number of tokens.
future_direction: Investigate how the presence of simple incomplete solutions affects the formation of more complex circuits in language modeling and other rich learning settings.
papers.abstract: Large language models have the ability to generate text that mimics patterns in their inputs. We introduce a simple Markov Chain sequence modeling task in order to study how this in-context learning (ICL) capability emerges. In our setting, each example is sampled from a Markov chain drawn from a prior distribution over Markov chains. Transformers trained on this task form \emph{statistical induction heads} which compute accurate next-token probabilities given the bigram statistics of the context. During the course of training, models pass through multiple phases: after an initial stage in which predictions are uniform, they learn to sub-optimally predict using in-context single-token statistics (unigrams); then, there is a rapid phase transition to the correct in-context bigram solution. We conduct an empirical and theoretical investigation of this multi-phase process, showing how successful learning results from the interaction between the transformer's layers, and uncovering evidence that the presence of the simpler unigram solution may delay formation of the final bigram solution. We examine how learning is affected by varying the prior distribution over Markov chains, and consider the generalization of our in-context learning of Markov chains (ICL-MC) task to $n$-grams for $n > 2$.

papers.title: Scaling Laws Under the Microscope: Predicting Transformer Performance from Small Scale Experiments
papers.research_question: Can scaling laws be used to predict the performance of larger transformer models from small-scale experiments, and how reliable are they across different NLP tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Scaling laws can be used to predict the performance of larger models for some NLP tasks, but they require careful hyperparameter tuning and do not consistently appear across all tasks.
papers.conclusion: Scaling laws are beneficial for debugging model convergence and predicting model behavior when they emerge at small scale, but revealing them requires careful control over hyperparameters and convergence conditions.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling laws emerge at pretraining time for both MLM and PMI objectives with high goodness-of-fit.
At finetuning time, scaling laws emerge only in some tasks, possibly depending on task similarity to pretraining and amount of data.
Hyperparameter tuning is crucial for revealing precise scaling laws, especially at smaller scales.
Scaling laws can be used for model selection when goodness-of-fit is high (R^2 > 0.95).
Revealing scaling laws incurs overhead from multiple runs and hyperparameter tuning, partially offsetting computational benefits.
papers.limitation:
Focused on small-scale models, with no empirical evidence for models that are significantly larger.
Analyzed encoder-only models, leaving decoder-based models for future work.
Analyzed 9 English-only datasets, none evaluating generation capabilities.
It remains unclear why scaling laws do not apply to all downstream tasks.
future_direction: Determine if predictions remain accurate when extrapolating over multiple orders-of-magnitude.
Study decoder-based models and generation capabilities.
Investigate why scaling laws do not apply to all tasks.
papers.abstract: Neural scaling laws define a predictable relationship between a model's parameter count and its performance after training in the form of a power law. However, most research to date has not explicitly investigated whether scaling laws can be used to accelerate model development. In this work, we perform such an empirical investigation across a wide range of language understanding tasks, starting from models with as few as 10K parameters, and evaluate downstream performance across 9 language understanding tasks. We find that scaling laws emerge at finetuning time in some NLP tasks, and that they can also be exploited for debugging convergence when training large models. Moreover, for tasks where scaling laws exist, they can be used to predict the performance of larger models, which enables effective model selection. However, revealing scaling laws requires careful hyperparameter tuning and multiple runs for the purpose of uncertainty estimation, which incurs additional overhead, partially offsetting the computational benefits.

papers.title: Large Language Models Encode Semantics and Alignment in Linearly Separable Representations
papers.research_question: To what extent do large language models encode high-level semantic information in linearly separable representations across domains and alignment behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode high-level semantics and alignment behaviors in linearly separable representations, enabling effective latent-space guardrails for safety.
papers.conclusion: LLMs organize high-level semantics and alignment in linearly separable subspaces, motivating geometry-aware tools for safer deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic representations become increasingly linearly separable in deeper layers.
Linear separability persists even when domain-specific keywords are masked.
Instruction following (e.g., chain-of-thought) induces linearly separable representations.
Safety-aligned models show separable clusters for benign and harmful prompts.
A lightweight MLP guardrail on hidden states improves refusal rates on adversarial prompts.
future_direction: Adversarial perturbation studies for causal validation
Axis-orthogonality tests for linear representations
Further research on information distribution across architectures
papers.abstract: Understanding the latent space geometry of large language models (LLMs) is key to interpreting their behavior and improving alignment. Yet it remains unclear to what extent LLMs linearly organize representations related to semantic understanding. To explore this, we conduct a large-scale empirical study of hidden representations in 11 autoregressive models across six scientific topics. We find that high-level semantic information consistently resides in low-dimensional subspaces that form linearly separable representations across domains. This separability becomes more pronounced in deeper layers and under prompts that elicit structured reasoning or alignment behavior$\unicode{x2013}$even when surface content remains unchanged. These findings motivate geometry-aware tools that operate directly in latent space to detect and mitigate harmful and adversarial content. As a proof of concept, we train an MLP probe on final-layer hidden states as a lightweight latent-space guardrail. This approach substantially improves refusal rates on malicious queries and prompt injections that bypass both the model's built-in safety alignment and external token-level filters.

papers.title: Polysemanticity and Capacity in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What are the causes of polysemanticity (individual neurons representing multiple unrelated features) in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of feature capacity to explain polysemanticity, showing that optimal capacity allocation in a toy model leads to monosemantic representation of important features, polysemantic representation of less important features, and ignoring of least important features, and characterizes the geometry of efficient embedding matrices.
papers.conclusion: The study of polysemanticity through feature capacity explains the sharp pinning of features to 0 or 1 capacity and reveals the block-semi-orthogonal geometry of efficient embedding matrices, suggesting architectural differences can control polysemanticity.
papers.key_findings:
Optimal capacity allocation tends to monosemantically represent the most important features, polysemantically represent less important features (in proportion to their impact on the loss), and entirely ignore the least important features.
Polysemanticity is more prevalent when the inputs have higher kurtosis or sparsity.
Polysemanticity is more prevalent in some architectures than others.
Efficient embedding matrices have a block-semi-orthogonal structure, with blocks corresponding to polytope structures found in prior work.
Differences in architecture can lead to different block sizes, which could provide a way to control the extent of polysemanticity.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on superposition as a cause of polysemanticity and does not study other causes such as rotated embeddings.
papers.abstract: Individual neurons in neural networks often represent a mixture of unrelated features. This phenomenon, called polysemanticity, can make interpreting neural networks more difficult and so we aim to understand its causes. We propose doing so through the lens of feature \emph{capacity}, which is the fractional dimension each feature consumes in the embedding space. We show that in a toy model the optimal capacity allocation tends to monosemantically represent the most important features, polysemantically represent less important features (in proportion to their impact on the loss), and entirely ignore the least important features. Polysemanticity is more prevalent when the inputs have higher kurtosis or sparsity and more prevalent in some architectures than others. Given an optimal allocation of capacity, we go on to study the geometry of the embedding space. We find a block-semi-orthogonal structure, with differing block sizes in different models, highlighting the impact of model architecture on the interpretability of its neurons.

papers.title: Challenges in Mechanistically Interpreting Model Representations
papers.research_question: What are the challenges in mechanistically interpreting model representations, and how do current mechanistic interpretability tools fall short in understanding complex behaviors like dishonesty?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes the importance of studying feature and behavior representations in models, performs an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in Mistral-7B, and shows that current mechanistic interpretability tools are insufficient for understanding such representations, advocating for new frameworks.
papers.conclusion: Studying representations for features and behaviors is crucial for understanding models, but current mechanistic interpretability tooling is inadequate for answering key questions about representations, necessitating new frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations for dishonesty can be found and used to steer model behavior, but they are not simply boosting generically dishonest tokens.
Continual injections of the dishonesty direction are required for open-ended dishonest generation, not just at the first token.
Direct logit attribution shows that directional injections affect many components, with MLPs having a more direct effect than attention heads.
Activation patching reveals that many components are involved in the dishonesty behavior, making sparse circuit analysis difficult and less helpful.
Current mechanistic interpretability tooling (e.g., patching) is insufficient for understanding how representations are formed and how they affect long-term generation.
papers.limitation: Patching methods (activation and path patching) do not rigorously prove that circuits found are indeed reserved to that task, and patching only one component at a time might not isolate components if multiple perform the same job.
future_direction: Study how different components interact with representations and alter them.
Explore the training dynamics of a model and study the emergence of representations as a model trains.
Develop new frameworks to think about and study representations.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to understand AI models by reverse-engineering the exact algorithms neural networks learn. Most works in MI so far have studied behaviors and capabilities that are trivial and token-aligned. However, most capabilities important for safety and trust are not that trivial, which advocates for the study of hidden representations inside these networks as the unit of analysis. We formalize representations for features and behaviors, highlight their importance and evaluation, and perform an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in `Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1'. We justify that studying representations is an important and under-studied field, and highlight several challenges that arise while attempting to do so through currently established methods in MI, showing their insufficiency and advocating work on new frameworks for the same.

papers.title: LLM world models are mental: Output layer evidence of brittle world model use in LLM mechanical reasoning
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) construct and manipulate internal 'world models,' or do they rely solely on statistical associations represented as output layer token probabilities learned from data?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs show some ability to reason about mechanical systems (pulley systems) using heuristics like pulley counting and can differentiate functional from jumbled systems, but their internal representations are brittle and fail when the task requires understanding of nuanced structural connectivity, indicating limited world model use.
papers.conclusion: The findings offer mixed support for the view that LLMs reason over world models independently from output token probabilities. The brittleness of these representations, especially in Study 3, aligns with critiques emphasizing the lack of robustness and generality in current systems.
papers.key_findings:
In Study 1, LLMs performed above chance in estimating mechanical advantage (MA) and their estimates correlated with ground truth MA, but they relied on a pulley-counting heuristic and selectively attended to relevant features.
LLMs could distinguish functional from non-functional (jumbled) pulley systems with high accuracy (F1=0.8) in Study 2.
In Study 3, LLMs failed to differentiate functional from non-functional (but connected) pulley systems, performing at chance level (F1=0.46).
The results suggest LLMs have some latent knowledge of pulley systems but lack robust internal models for nuanced structural reasoning.
The brittleness of these representations aligns with critiques emphasizing the lack of robustness and generality in current systems.
papers.limitation:
Uncertainty regarding whether tested pulley stimuli are truly out-of-distribution; exposure during training cannot be ruled out.
Difficulty deconfounding output layer token representations from potential latent world models represented in network weights without combining with interpretability research.
future_direction: Future work should further deconfound pulley count from MA and employ novel or synthetic diagramming languages to limit reliance on familiar formats like TikZ.
Extending the paradigm to other physical systems (e.g., levers, gear trains) may help assess the breadth of these internal representations.
Integrating the present approach with interpretability research may help elucidate the network circuits underlying reasoning over world models.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) construct and manipulate internal world models, or do they rely solely on statistical associations represented as output layer token probabilities? We adapt cognitive science methodologies from human mental models research to test LLMs on pulley system problems using TikZ-rendered stimuli. Study 1 examines whether LLMs can estimate mechanical advantage (MA). State-of-the-art models performed marginally but significantly above chance, and their estimates correlated significantly with ground-truth MA. Significant correlations between number of pulleys and model estimates suggest that models employed a pulley counting heuristic, without necessarily simulating pulley systems to derive precise values. Study 2 tested this by probing whether LLMs represent global features crucial to MA estimation. Models evaluated a functionally connected pulley system against a fake system with randomly placed components. Without explicit cues, models identified the functional system as having greater MA with F1=0.8, suggesting LLMs could represent systems well enough to differentiate jumbled from functional systems. Study 3 built on this by asking LLMs to compare functional systems with matched systems which were connected up but which transferred no force to the weight; LLMs identified the functional system with F1=0.46, suggesting random guessing. Insofar as they may generalize, these findings are compatible with the notion that LLMs manipulate internal world models, sufficient to exploit statistical associations between pulley count and MA (Study 1), and to approximately represent system components' spatial relations (Study 2). However, they may lack the facility to reason over nuanced structural connectivity (Study 3). We conclude by advocating the utility of cognitive scientific methods to evaluate the world-modeling capacities of artificial intelligence systems.

papers.title: Decomposing Representation Space into Interpretable Subspaces with Unsupervised Learning
papers.research_question: Can we find interpretable subspaces in neural representations in an unsupervised way? To what extent are different aspects organized in separate subspaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an unsupervised method (NDM) to decompose representation space into interpretable subspaces, showing that these subspaces align with known circuit variables and can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis.
papers.conclusion: Unsupervised decomposition of representation space into interpretable subspaces is possible, and these subspaces can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis, offering a new perspective on understanding model internals.
papers.key_findings:
NDM can find interpretable subspaces without supervision, as shown in toy models and real language models.
Subspaces found by NDM align with variables in known circuits in GPT-2, as evidenced by high Gini coefficients in subspace patching experiments.
The method scales to 2B models, finding separate subspaces for context and parametric knowledge routing.
Qualitative analysis shows that subspaces are consistent and interpretable across different inputs.
papers.limitation: The method can get stuck in local minima, leading to sub-optimal subspace partitions.
future_direction: hierarchical structure of subspaces
more flexible searching over dimension configurations
applying the method to larger models and more tasks
papers.abstract: Understanding internal representations of neural models is a core interest of mechanistic interpretability. Due to its large dimensionality, the representation space can encode various aspects about inputs. To what extent are different aspects organized and encoded in separate subspaces? Is it possible to find these ``natural'' subspaces in a purely unsupervised way? Somewhat surprisingly, we can indeed achieve this and find interpretable subspaces by a seemingly unrelated training objective. Our method, neighbor distance minimization (NDM), learns non-basis-aligned subspaces in an unsupervised manner. Qualitative analysis shows subspaces are interpretable in many cases, and encoded information in obtained subspaces tends to share the same abstract concept across different inputs, making such subspaces similar to ``variables'' used by the model. We also conduct quantitative experiments using known circuits in GPT-2; results show a strong connection between subspaces and circuit variables. We also provide evidence showing scalability to 2B models by finding separate subspaces mediating context and parametric knowledge routing. Viewed more broadly, our findings offer a new perspective on understanding model internals and building circuits.

papers.title: Mechanistic Knobs in LLMs: Retrieving and Steering High-Order Semantic Features via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can internal features in Large Language Models be linked to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering high-order semantic features in LLMs, enabling precise, bidirectional behavior control and identifying the Functional Faithfulness effect where interventions induce coherent shifts across linguistic dimensions.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, providing a robust mechanistic path for regulating complex AI behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based features allow precise steering of personality traits in LLMs, enabling bidirectional control.
The method outperforms Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) in stability and performance, with higher validity rates.
Functional Faithfulness effect is observed where steering on a feature induces systematic behavioral shifts aligned with the target semantic attribute.
Retrieved features are semantically interpretable and causally effective for model behavior regulation.
LLM internal representations of personality traits align with human psychological frameworks, as shown through social intelligence evaluations.
papers.abstract: Recent work in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has enabled the identification and intervention of internal features in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, a persistent challenge lies in linking such internal features to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation. In this paper, we propose a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering semantically interpretable internal features associated with high-level linguistic behaviors. Our method employs a contrastive feature retrieval pipeline based on controlled semantic oppositions, combing statistical activation analysis and generation-based validation to distill monosemantic functional features from sparse activation spaces. Using the Big Five personality traits as a case study, we demonstrate that our method enables precise, bidirectional steering of model behavior while maintaining superior stability and performance compared to existing activation steering methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). We further identify an empirical effect, which we term Functional Faithfulness, whereby intervening on a specific internal feature induces coherent and predictable shifts across multiple linguistic dimensions aligned with the target semantic attribute. Our findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, and provide a novel, robust mechanistic path for the regulation of complex AI behaviors.

papers.title: Understanding sparse autoencoder scaling in the presence of feature manifolds
papers.research_question: How do feature manifolds influence the scaling behavior of sparse autoencoders, and can they cause pathological scaling where SAEs allocate too many latents to common manifolds at the expense of discovering rarer features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper adapts a capacity-allocation model to sparse autoencoders, revealing that feature manifolds can lead to pathological scaling where SAEs allocate excessive latents to common manifolds, potentially hindering feature discovery.
papers.conclusion: The work frames the problem of SAE scaling and identifies conditions for pathological scaling, but it remains uncertain whether real SAEs are in this regime due to unknown feature geometry and frequency distributions.
papers.key_findings:
The model recovers distinct scaling regimes for SAEs: one where feature discovery keeps pace with latent count, and another where latents accumulate on common feature manifolds.
When the per-feature loss scaling exponent β is less than the feature frequency exponent α, SAEs enter a pathological regime where they learn far fewer features than the number of latents.
Experiments on synthetic manifolds show that the loss scaling curve depends on manifold geometry; some manifolds allow gradual loss reduction with more latents, while others saturate quickly.
Analysis of real SAEs (Gemma Scope and Inception-v1) shows some latents with high cosine similarity, but evidence for pathological tiling is inconclusive.
The presence of radial variation in feature manifolds may cause SAEs to learn basis-like solutions rather than tiling, suggesting pathological scaling might not occur in practice.
papers.limitation:
The assumptions of feature-specific latents, decoder respect for subspaces, and orthogonal feature subspaces may not hold in practice (e.g., due to feature absorption and non-orthogonality).
The model assumes power-law distributions for feature frequencies and loss scaling, which may not accurately reflect real data.
The question of whether SAEs are in the pathological regime is not resolved due to uncertainty about real feature geometries and frequencies.
future_direction: Estimating the feature frequency exponent α and loss scaling exponent β for real SAEs.
Studying the geometry of real feature manifolds to better understand SAE scaling behavior.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) model the activations of a neural network as linear combinations of sparsely occurring directions of variation (latents). The ability of SAEs to reconstruct activations follows scaling laws w.r.t. the number of latents. In this work, we adapt a capacity-allocation model from the neural scaling literature (Brill, 2024) to understand SAE scaling, and in particular, to understand how "feature manifolds" (multi-dimensional features) influence scaling behavior. Consistent with prior work, the model recovers distinct scaling regimes. Notably, in one regime, feature manifolds have the pathological effect of causing SAEs to learn far fewer features in data than there are latents in the SAE. We provide some preliminary discussion on whether or not SAEs are in this pathological regime in the wild.

papers.title: Probing and Steering Evaluation Awareness of Language Models
papers.research_question: Can language models internally distinguish between testing and deployment phases (evaluation awareness), and how can this capability be probed and steered?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that evaluation awareness is linearly represented in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and can be extracted using linear probes, and that steering with evaluation-awareness-relevant SAE features can partially uncover sandbagging behavior.
papers.conclusion: Modern language models develop internal representations that distinguish evaluation from deployment contexts; current evaluation scenarios may be readily identifiable as artificial, highlighting the need for more realistic evaluation frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes trained on model activations can detect evaluation contexts with high AUROC scores (up to 0.829).
The probes generalize across different evaluation and deployment prompt datasets.
Current safety evaluation prompts (e.g., for deception) are often classified as test-like, suggesting models may recognize them as artificial evaluations.
Steering with SAE features related to evaluation awareness can partially recover sandbagged capabilities on the WMDP benchmark, but linear probe steering had minimal impact.
Evaluation awareness representations are more distinctly encoded in earlier model layers (e.g., layers 23-24).
papers.limitation:
The evaluation awareness observed in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct may be less pronounced than in frontier models, raising concerns about generalizability.
Linear probes may not capture the full complexity of evaluation awareness, which may not be strictly one-dimensionally linear.
The experimental setup is a significant simplification compared to real-world scenarios of concern (e.g., extended agentic backdoor honeypots).
Steering attempts using linear probes and SAE features showed limited success in modifying sandbagging behavior.
future_direction: Comprehensive red-teaming with alternative probe training methods (e.g., logistic regression, PCA, non-linear probes).
Leveraging probes to enhance the realism of scheming honeypots via automated prompt authenticity enhancement.
Integrating probe-based detection into control protocols as a low-latency whitebox monitoring system.
papers.abstract: Language models can distinguish between testing and deployment phases -- a capability known as evaluation awareness. This has significant safety and policy implications, potentially undermining the reliability of evaluations that are central to AI governance frameworks and voluntary industry commitments. In this paper, we study evaluation awareness in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct. We show that linear probes can separate real-world evaluation and deployment prompts, suggesting that current models internally represent this distinction. We also find that current safety evaluations are correctly classified by the probes, suggesting that they already appear artificial or inauthentic to models. Our findings underscore the importance of ensuring trustworthy evaluations and understanding deceptive capabilities. More broadly, our work showcases how model internals may be leveraged to support blackbox methods in safety audits, especially for future models more competent at evaluation awareness and deception.

papers.title: Interpretability With Accurate Small Models
papers.research_question: How can we minimize the trade-off between interpretability (small model size) and classification accuracy? The paper proposes that modifying the training distribution can lead to higher accuracy for small models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a model-agnostic technique that adaptively samples training data to identify an optimal training distribution, thereby improving the accuracy of small, interpretable models without increasing their size.
papers.conclusion: The proposed adaptive sampling technique effectively minimizes the trade-off between interpretability and accuracy, enabling the construction of highly accurate small-sized models across various model families and datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Modifying the training distribution can significantly improve the accuracy of small models, with F1-score improvements sometimes exceeding 100%.
The technique reduces the optimization problem to a fixed set of eight variables, independent of data dimensionality, making it scalable.
The method is model-agnostic and demonstrated effectiveness with decision trees, linear probability models, and gradient boosted models.
The optimal training distribution for a small model can differ from the test distribution, challenging the conventional wisdom that train and test data must come from the same distribution.
The approach uses Bayesian Optimization (Tree-structured Parzen Estimator) and an Infinite Beta Mixture Model for density estimation to efficiently search for the optimal distribution.
future_direction: Applying the technique to model compression.
Exploring other density representations and optimization methods.
papers.abstract: Models often need to be constrained to a certain size for them to be considered interpretable. For example, a decision tree of depth 5 is much easier to understand than one of depth 50. Limiting model size, however, often reduces accuracy. We suggest a practical technique that minimizes this trade-off between interpretability and classification accuracy. This enables an arbitrary learning algorithm to produce highly accurate small-sized models. Our technique identifies the training data distribution to learn from that leads to the highest accuracy for a model of a given size. We represent the training distribution as a combination of sampling schemes. Each scheme is defined by a parameterized probability mass function applied to the segmentation produced by a decision tree. An Infinite Mixture Model with Beta components is used to represent a combination of such schemes. The mixture model parameters are learned using Bayesian Optimization. Under simplistic assumptions, we would need to optimize for O(d) variables for a distribution over a d-dimensional input space, which is cumbersome for most real-world data. However, we show that our technique significantly reduces this number to a fixed set of eight variables at the cost of relatively cheap preprocessing. The proposed technique is flexible: it is model-agnostic, i.e., it may be applied to the learning algorithm for any model family, and it admits a general notion of model size. We demonstrate its effectiveness using multiple real-world datasets to construct decision trees, linear probability models and gradient boosted models with different sizes. We observe significant improvements in the F1-score in most instances, exceeding an improvement of 100% in some cases.

papers.title: A Mathematical Philosophy of Explanations in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the nature of explanations in mechanistic interpretability, and how can we define and demarcate mechanistic interpretability as a scientific practice?
papers.core_contribution: The paper defines mechanistic interpretability as the practice of producing model-level, ontic, causal-mechanistic, and falsifiable explanations of neural networks, and argues that the Principle of Explanatory Optimism is a necessary precondition for its success.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mechanistic interpretability is a valuable scientific practice for understanding neural networks, grounded in the Explanatory View and dependent on the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, and provides a framework for defining and pursuing faithful explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The Explanatory View Hypothesis posits that neural networks contain implicit explanations of their behavior that can be extracted and understood.
Explanatory faithfulness is defined as the extent to which an explanation matches the model's internal mechanisms (ur-explanations), not just its input-output behavior.
Mechanistic interpretability is formally defined as seeking explanations that are model-level, ontic, causal-mechanistic, and falsifiable.
Mechanistic interpretability has inherent limits due to the value-ladenness and theory-ladenness of explanations, and its focus on model-level explanations excludes system-level complexities.
The Principle of Explanatory Optimism states that the algorithmic structure learned by generalizing neural networks is human-understandable, and without this assumption, mechanistic interpretability is intractable.
papers.limitation:
Explanations in mechanistic interpretability are value-laden, as the choice of precision and metrics depends on the interpreter's goals and values.
Explanations are theory-laden, as interpretability methods rely on theoretical commitments (e.g., sparse autoencoders assume sparsity and linearity).
Mechanistic interpretability focuses on model-level explanations, but AI systems involve additional components beyond the model, limiting the scope of MI for understanding system behavior.
future_direction: Increased focus on criteria that make explanations accessible to diverse humans, involving human-computer interaction and social sciences.
Development of a new field focusing on system-level explanations, building on mechanistic interpretability.
Collaboration between philosophy, computational complexity, and machine learning to investigate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to understand neural net- works through causal explanations. We argue for the Explanatory View Hypothesis: that Mechanistic Interpretability re- search is a principled approach to understanding models be- cause neural networks contain implicit explanations which can be extracted and understood. We hence show that Explanatory Faithfulness, an assessment of how well an explanation fits a model, is well-defined. We propose a definition of Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks, allowing us to distinguish MI from other interpretability paradigms and detail MI’s inherent limits. We formulate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, a conjecture which we argue is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.

papers.title: Why Can GPT Learn In-Context? Language Models Secretly Perform Gradient Descent as Meta-Optimizers
papers.research_question: What is the working mechanism of in-context learning in GPT models? The paper investigates whether in-context learning can be understood as a form of implicit finetuning.
papers.core_contribution: The paper explains in-context learning as implicit finetuning by showing a dual form between Transformer attention and gradient descent, and provides empirical evidence that ICL behaves similarly to explicit finetuning.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning can be understood as a process of meta-optimization, specifically as implicit finetuning, and this understanding can inspire improved model designs like momentum-based attention.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent.
In-context learning updates attention outputs and weights in a direction similar to explicit finetuning.
In-context learning covers most of the correct predictions made by a finetuned model.
In-context learning and finetuning pay similar attention to training tokens.
A momentum-based attention mechanism, inspired by the dual form, improves performance over vanilla attention in language modeling and ICL tasks.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to Transformer-based architectures and does not cover other architectures like LSTMs.
The dual form is derived using a relaxed linear attention approximation, and the mechanism of standard Transformer attention may be more complex.
Due to computational cost, the analysis is limited to models up to 2.7B parameters and does not include larger models.
The analysis is based only on classification tasks and does not consider other task types like multiple choice or open-ended generation.
future_direction: Study in-context learning in non-Transformer architectures.
Investigate the mechanism of standard Transformer attention without the linear approximation.
Extend the analysis to larger models (e.g., GPT 13B).
Investigate in-context learning on other task types like multiple choice and open-ended generation.
papers.abstract: Large pretrained language models have shown surprising in-context learning (ICL) ability. With a few demonstration input-label pairs, they can predict the label for an unseen input without parameter updates. Despite the great success in performance, its working mechanism still remains an open question. In this paper, we explain language models as meta-optimizers and understand in-context learning as implicit finetuning. Theoretically, we figure out that Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent. On top of it, we understand ICL as follows: GPT first produces meta-gradients according to the demonstration examples, and then these meta-gradients are applied to the original GPT to build an ICL model. We comprehensively compare the behaviors of in-context learning and explicit finetuning on real tasks to provide empirical evidence that supports our understanding. Experimental results show that in-context learning behaves similarly to explicit finetuning from multiple perspectives. Inspired by the dual form between Transformer attention and gradient descent, we design a momentum-based attention by analogy with gradient descent with momentum. The improved performance over vanilla attention further supports our understanding from another perspective, and more importantly, shows the potential to utilize our understanding for future model design. The code is available at https://aka.ms/icl.

papers.title: Bridging the Dimensional Chasm: Uncover Layer-wise Dimensional Reduction in Transformers through Token Correlation
papers.research_question: How do token representations evolve from high-dimensional embeddings to low-dimensional structures in Transformers, and what is the relationship between geometric properties (like intrinsic dimension) and model performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a geometric framework that tracks token dynamics across Transformer layers, revealing an expansion-contraction pattern and a negative correlation between the working space dimension (dmodel) and model performance.
papers.conclusion: Transformers mediate between high-dimensional machine working spaces and low-dimensional semantic manifolds, and the introduced quantities (dmodel, dmachine) offer a unifying framework for model assessment and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
